title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest leans on the freshest 2025–2026 evidence across your tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative angles on HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Sources (PubMed, JAMA/Nature, NIH/ClinicalTrials.gov, AASM and more) are linked as chips under each section. Informational only — run anything you'd act on past a clinician first.

sections.topic: Anti-Aging — Supplements, Topicals & the Longevity Hype
sections.body:
The through-line from this month's reviews: **target engagement is easy, proven anti-aging is not.** Expect modest, endpoint-specific effects and be wary of single-pill "longevity" promises.

- **Rapamycin — safe, but not yet proven to slow aging.** The **PEARL** trial (the longest human rapamycin study to date, 48 weeks, weekly 5–10 mg vs. placebo in ~129 healthy adults) found intermittent low-dose rapamycin was **relatively safe** and linked to gains in **lean tissue mass and less pain in women**, but it did **not** demonstrate longevity/healthspan efficacy — the primary visceral-fat endpoint wasn't met. Off-label use for "anti-aging" is still ahead of the evidence.
- **Supplement scorecard.** A new comparative review (Jan 2016–Apr 2026) ranks the big three: **urolithin A** has the most *coherent* profile — aligned mechanism, biomarker and early functional data for mitochondrial health, muscle endurance and immune aging. **NR/NMN** reliably raise NAD+ biomarkers but show **inconsistent** clinical benefit. **Spermidine** remains biologically plausible but clinically unvalidated.
- **Taurine, pending.** The randomized **TauAge** trial (4 g/day taurine for 6 months in adults 55–75, epigenetic-clock and proteomic aging readouts) has **completed** — results not yet reported, so treat taurine "reverses aging" headlines as unproven for now.

Bottom line: prefer interventions with human RCTs, expect small effects, and don't stack unproven longevity pills expecting additive gains.

sections.body:
If retinoids irritate your skin, 2026 gives the **retinoid-alternative** story its best data yet — led by **bakuchiol**, with **exosome-delivered** formulas still early.

- **Bakuchiol (strongest evidence).** A **double-blind, vehicle-controlled** 84-day trial (73 participants) found topical bakuchiol significantly improved **wrinkle severity, hyperpigmentation, pore size and radiance** versus placebo — echoing earlier head-to-head data showing it works like retinol but is **better tolerated**. A separate randomized sensitive-skin study of a **supramolecular bakuchiol + Terminalia chebula** formula reported reduced wrinkle area and improved barrier measures over 28 days.
- **Exosome delivery (promising but preliminary).** An open-label study of **retinal (retinaldehyde) encapsulated in a biomimetic exosome** in 20 women showed improvements in lines/wrinkles, tone and texture at every visit with **no product-related adverse events** — but it was small and uncontrolled. A ginseng-exosome + microneedle photoaging platform has only a **30-person pilot**. Treat exosome skincare as investigational, not a proven retinoid replacement.

Practical read: bakuchiol is a reasonable, well-tolerated daily option for photoaging; exosome products are worth watching, not banking on.

sections.body:
The 2026 message stays consistent: HIIT is a **time-efficient cardio and cardiometabolic** win for women — but **pair it with strength work**, because intervals alone don't fully cover functional fitness.

- **Big-picture meta-analysis.** A new systematic review & meta-analysis (**19 RCTs, ~646 middle-aged and older women**) found HIIT **significantly improves VO2max** (high certainty) but had **limited effect on muscle strength and physical function** — the authors conclude HIIT alone is insufficient to comprehensively improve functional performance.
- **Older women RCT.** A supervised HIIT program (3×/week) produced significant gains in **aerobic capacity, lower-limb strength and mobility (Timed Up-and-Go)**, plus drops in body-fat and visceral-fat indices and better quality of life — no major adverse events.
- **Heart benefits in obesity.** In women with obesity, 8 weeks of **4×4-min HIIT** improved **myocardial work efficiency** (less wasted work) more than moderate continuous training — a signal for targeting early, subclinical cardiac dysfunction.
- **Postmenopausal metabolism.** A 12-week trial comparing **HIIT vs. concurrent (HIIT + resistance)** training found **both** cut triglycerides, LDL, glucose and insulin resistance, but the **concurrent group lost more body weight and fat** — reinforcing that adding resistance work pays off.

Bottom line: use HIIT for cardio and metabolic gains, but blend in resistance training for strength, body composition and functional independence.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** stays the evidence-based **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). This week's trials show how to make it work better — and even how it may **delay surgery**.

- **Intensive prehab can postpone the OR.** An RCT (Int Urogynecol J, Mar 2026) of **6-week intensive preoperative PFMT** vs. education-only in 90 women awaiting sling surgery found large improvements in **muscle strength (Modified Oxford, d=0.85)** and **symptom severity (ISI, d=0.90)** — and in **43% of the training group the planned surgery was postponed.** A low-risk, cost-efficient step before opting for surgery.
- **Add electrical stimulation for very weak muscles.** A multicentre, double-blind RCT found that adding **sEMG-triggered intravaginal electrical stimulation** to supervised PFMT produced **earlier, greater and longer-lasting** gains than PFMT + sham: at 12 months, larger drops in weekly leakage, pad use and ICIQ-SF, with **65% vs. 18%** reporting clinically meaningful improvement.
- **Telehealth works if you can self-cue.** In 50 women able to contract via instruction and self-palpation, **PFMT by teleconsultation** beat an educational approach on SUI severity, leakage episodes, pad use and quality of life — a viable remote option.

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps.** Confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback; supervised programs generally outperform unsupervised ones.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
Read "alternative" as **precision/integrative approaches alongside standard HER2-targeted therapy** — not a replacement for it. The most concrete 2026 news is a **p53-directed drug**, not a supplement.

- **Reactivating mutant p53 (PYNNACLE).** The phase 1/2 **PYNNACLE** basket trial of **rezatapopt** — a first-in-class oral reactivator that refolds the **TP53 Y220C** mutant back toward wild-type — is enrolling ~114 patients across tumor cohorts (2000 mg once daily). In the **breast-cancer cohort (n=11)** the interim overall response rate was **18%**, including HER2-positive cases; earlier phase 1 breast data showed confirmed responses too. Eligibility requires TP53 Y220C **and** KRAS wild-type — so genotyping matters.
- **HER2;p53 co-mutants and T-DXd.** Preclinical work shows HER2/TP53 co-mutated tumors are **resistant to neratinib** but stay **sensitive to the TOP1-inhibitor payload in trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd)** via increased histone acetylation/chromatin accessibility. The **neratinib + T-DXd** combination is being tested clinically (NCI-ETCTN **NCT05372614**).
- **A TP53-stratified chemo trial.** The ongoing **p53 Breast Cancer Trial** (NCT02965950) stratifies patients by TP53 status and uses dose-dense cyclophosphamide, with a first-line HER2-positive metastatic arm.

Important framing: much of this is **early or genotype-specific**. Integrative add-ons (nutrition, supplements) should be **coordinated with your oncology team** for interaction risk — and never substituted for HER2-targeted therapy.

sections.body:
For restless or disjointed sleep, 2026 guidance keeps **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements.**

- **CBT-I is first-line.** Major guidelines (AASM; European Insomnia Guideline) recommend **cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)** — stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive restructuring, sleep-hygiene education — as the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia at any age, delivered **in-person or digitally**. Medication is best reserved for those who can't access CBT-I, still have symptoms after it, or need a short-term adjunct.
- **If medication is needed.** For **short-term (≤4 weeks)** use, benzodiazepine receptor agonists and the **dual orexin receptor antagonist daridorexant** are supported; low-dose sedating antidepressants are an option. **Melatonin is *not* recommended for chronic insomnia** — reserve it for **circadian problems** (jet lag, shift work), with prolonged-release melatonin an option in adults ≥55.
- **Magnesium — mixed at best.** A 2026 systematic review of RCTs concluded current evidence **does not support routine oral magnesium for insomnia**; any benefit is modest, inconsistent, and low-certainty (it's more useful for nocturnal leg cramps that fragment sleep).

Best-practice habits for disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If disruption persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea / restless legs** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or app-based).
